activity: Rose is watching a big game with family and friends.
story:
Rose went to the big game with Dad. There were many people there. "One, two, three," said Rose. "So many feet!" The crowd stood up and clapped.

Rose could not see the ball. She peeked between two big legs. She saw a little bit. Then the legs moved. Now she saw nothing at all. "Why can't I see?" she asked. Dad said, "Look in front of you." A tall man was standing there. His back was in the way. That was why!

Rose looked around. She saw a bench. She climbed up on it. Now she was tall too. She could see the whole field! The ball went far, far away. "The man was in my way," said Rose. "Now I am up high. I can see!"

Uncle Sam held up his phone. "Smile, Rose!" Rose smiled big. Click. "Can I peek at the picture?" she asked. Yes, she could. There she was, on the good bench, smiling.

The game ended. Everyone yelled "Hooray!" Rose clapped and clapped. She looked at the bench one more time. "Good bench," said Rose. "See you next game!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Isla sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later.
story:
Isla wants to paint a cat at daycare. Yesterday she painted a sun, and Teacher Jo hung it on the wall. Today the sun is dry, so it can hang there now.

Isla paints her cat. It is orange with a long tail. The paint is wet. It drips a little on her hand. "The paint is slow to dry," says Teacher Jo. "Your cat can hang up later." So Isla sets the cat on the shelf to dry.

Isla waits. She has a snack. She plays with blocks. She looks at her cat again. Now the paint feels dry! Teacher Jo hangs it next to the sun. Isla smiles. Then she sees something. Her cat's tail made a spot on the paper. It looks like a little orange dog! "Two animals," says Isla. "Tomorrow I can paint a house for them both."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Nathan sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the days of the week, the months and the idea that a calendar shows when things happen.
story:
Nathan did not want to sleep. He had one big question. "When is my birthday?" he asked Dad.

Dad did not just tell him. He held up the big calendar by Nathan's bed. "Find it," said Dad. Nathan put his finger on the paper. He saw rows of little squares. Some said Monday, some said Tuesday, all the way to Sunday. Dad turned a page. Each page was a month. "October," said Nathan. Then he saw it. His name was written on a square! The square said Saturday, October the tenth.

"So my birthday is a Saturday," said Nathan. "Today is Tuesday." He tapped two little squares. "I sleep two more times, and then it comes!" Dad kissed his head. "That is right," he said. Outside, the window was frozen at the corner, white and cold. Nathan's finger tapped the glass. It did not hurt. It just felt like ice.

Dad tucked him in. "Good night, birthday boy," he said. Nathan smiled at the calendar. "Good night, Saturday," Nathan whispered. "Come fast."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Everly sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle.
story:
Everly wanted to build a barn at daycare. The toy farm animals needed a home. The little cow waited on the rug.

She picked a round block. It was orange like a ball. She stacked blocks on top of it. The tower wobbled. Then it fell down. The round block rolled away under the table.

Everly crawled over and gave it a pull. It slid out with a soft bump. Then she tried a square block. It had flat sides. She stacked more blocks on it. The tower stood still. "It stays!" she said.

Milo came over with sad eyes. His pig had no home either. "Build with the flat ones," Everly said. She handed him a long block. "This one is like a door." They put a triangle on top for the roof. It looked just like a real barn.

Milo pressed a squishy triangle into the play dough. It left a triangle hole. Everly clapped. The farmer pig went inside. So did the cow. "Good night, farm," Everly whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Jasper sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects.
story:
Jasper ran to the playground with his grandma. "Stay near me," Grandma said. Jasper held her hand.

The sun was bright. The slide felt hot under Jasper's fingers. He pulled his hand back fast. "Ouch! It's hot!" Grandma touched the slide too. "Yes. Let's find a shady slide." The shady slide felt cool. Whee! Down went Jasper.

Near the fence, Jasper saw a tiny dog. The dog wagged its tail. Jasper wanted to pet it. A sharp stick lay on the ground by the fence. Jasper reached for the stick. Grandma picked it up first. "Sticks can poke. Let's leave it there." She put it behind the fence.

Then the dog did a funny thing. It rolled over, all four feet in the air. Jasper laughed and laughed. The dog's owner came with a leash. "You may pet his back," the owner said. Jasper petted the soft, warm fur.

"Time to walk home," said Grandma. Jasper held her hand all the way to the gate. "Bye, dog!" he called. The dog barked once, and Jasper smiled.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Gabriel sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the idea that plants and animals need food, water and a place to live.
story:
Gabriel ran out to the garden. The sun was bright. He saw a little brown bird on the path. It did not fly away. "Are you hungry?" Gabriel asked. "I think you are hungry!"

Gabriel looked at the bird. Then he looked at the flowers. They looked sad and droopy. "Why are you droopy?" he asked. He touched the dirt. It was dry, dry, dry. That was why! The flowers had no water.

Gablin got the watering can. He filled it up. He watered the flowers, one, two, three. He spilled some water on the path. The little bird hopped over. It took a drink! "You were thirsty too," said Gabriel. "Water is good for you!"

Then Gabriel found some seeds on the ground. He put them by the green bush. The bird flew to the bush. The bush was the bird's home. It ate the seeds and hid in the leaves. "You need food and water and a home," said Gabriel. "Just like my flowers!"

Dad called from the car. "Time to go, Gabriel!" Gabriel waved at the bird. "I will bring more water tomorrow," he said. The bird chirped from its bush.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Julia sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the idea that plants and animals need food, water and a place to live.
story:
Julia went out to the backyard. She saw a little bird on the fence. The bird looked thirsty. "Where does a bird get water?" Julia asked. She looked and looked. She did not see any water.

Julia found an old pie pan. She asked Dad to help. Dad filled the pan with water. They set it under the curly tree. The little bird flew down. It drank and drank. Then it splashed in its bath. Julia laughed and clapped.

The next day, the bird came back. It had a friend. Both birds drank from the pan. Julia saw the seeds on the ground too. The birds ate the seeds. Then they flew up into the tree. "Now they have water, food, and a home," Julia said. She waved to the birds in the curly branches.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Maria is making an art or craft project.
story:
Maria went to the art studio with her dad. A big sign on the wall said "Paint Day". Maria wanted to paint a cat. She got red paint, blue paint, and a brush.

She painted one ear. She painted two eyes. She painted three whiskers. Then she painted the cat's nose. The nose was red, but the cat's body was blue. Maria frowned. "My cat looks funny," she said. A boy named Tom laughed kindly. "A red nose on a blue cat? Silly cat!"

Maria looked at her paint cup. The red was all wet and shiny. Then she saw why. The paint was still wet, so her brush had dripped. "Wet paint drips," Maria said. "That is why I got a red dot." She got a clean brush and new paint.

She painted one ear, two eyes, three whiskers, and a big purple nose on purpose. Tom clapped. "Best silly cat ever!" Maria held it up high. "Meow!" she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Naomi is learning something new. What Naomi is learning: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done.
story:
Naomi went with Dad to the phone repair shop. Rain tapped on the big window. Naomi wanted to draw, but her tablet would not turn on.

The shop man smiled. "Let me teach you," he said. He showed Naomi the small button on the side. He pressed it. The screen lit up! "Your turn," he said. Naomi pressed the button herself. The screen was dark. She pressed it again, longer. The screen lit up like magic.

Then the man tapped the green square. A drawing app opened. Naomi drew a cat. She drew rain. She drew the shop man's big smile. When she was done, the man showed her the button again. Naomi pressed it. The screen went dark. She put the tablet in her bag, all by herself.

"Good job," the man said. Naomi pressed her hands together like a tiny button and smiled. "Zap!" she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Kayden sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help.
story:
Kayden went to the store with Mom. He wanted a soft brown bear. The bear sat high on the shelf. Kayden could not reach it.

"Can you help me, please?" Kayden asked the store man. The store man smiled. He reached up with a long pole. Down came the bear, soft as a cloud. "Thank you!" said Kayden. He hugged the bear tight.

Kayden walked fast with joy. He bumped a big stack of crayon boxes. Crash! The boxes fell like red and blue rain. "Sorry," said Kayden. The store man helped him sweep them up, one box, two boxes, three boxes. Then Mom said, "Say please one more time." Kayden held the bear up high. "Please can we take him home?" And home they went, Kayden waving the bear's soft paw. "Bye bye, store!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Felix sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green.
story:
Felix went to the store with Mama. He wanted a new cup. His old cup had a crack. It was the wrong cup for bedtime juice.

First they saw apples. The apples were red and round. Felix put one in the cart. Then they saw blueberries. The blueberries were blue and small. Mama said, "These look good." Felix helped her pick a box.

Felix looked for the cups. He walked slowly with Mama. He saw a green cup on a low shelf. He picked it up. The green cup had a bug on it. The bug was yellow and tiny. It was just a picture. Felix smiled at the little bug.

Then Felix did something. He put the green cup under the yellow light above the shelf. The yellow light made the cup look yellow too. The green was gone! Felix whispered, "Oh no." He took the cup away from the light. The cup was green again. Felix laughed. The light had played a trick.

Mama said, "That is a nice cup." Felix put the green cup in the cart. The yellow bug rode on top. At home, Mama washed the cup. Then she poured in juice. Felix took a big sip. "The bug cup is the best cup," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Isabella sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting.
story:
Isabella went to the library with her family. She wanted a book about ducks. But where were the duck books?

A shiny cart stood by the desk. Isabella touched it and the wheels went round. The cart rolled a little. Then ten books slid off, one by one.

"Look, Isabella," said the librarian. "Count with me." She bent down and picked up the books. "One, two, three." Isabella helped. "Four, five, six," she said. The librarian smiled. "Seven, eight, nine." One book was left. Isabella held it up. "Ten!" she said.

The last book was about ducks. Isabella laughed. "Did my hands find it?" she asked. "Yes," said the librarian. "Your counting found it too." Isabella hugged the duck book tight. "Quack," she said, very softly.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Charlotte is learning something new. What Charlotte is learning: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling.
story:
Charlotte was at her friend Mia's house. Mia's mom made warm toast. Charlotte wanted to butter it all by herself.

"Slow hands," said Mia's mom. "Slow, slow, slow."

Charlotte held the knife. The butter was too cold and hard. It would not spread. It tore the toast. Then Mia's mom set the butter dish near the sunny window. They waited. Charlotte counted, "One, two, three, four, five." The butter got soft and shiny. Now the knife slid over the toast, slow, slow, slow. The butter covered every corner.

Next came the milk. Charlotte poured too fast. Milk splashed onto the table. "Oops," she said. She washed her hands. She tried again. This time she poured just a little bit, then a little bit more. Not one drop spilled. Mia clapped.

"You did it," said Mia. Charlotte lifted her cup. "Milk for me," she said. "And toast for you."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Harrison is celebrating a birthday with family and friends.
story:
Harrison woke up at Grandma's house. Today he was three! He ran to the kitchen in his pajamas.

Grandma had a big cake on the table. "Not yet," she said with a smile. "We wait for the party."

Soon the door opened. Mom, Dad, Aunt Bee, and cousin Milo came in. They all shouted, "Happy birthday, Harrison!" Even his friend Zoe from next door came with a wrapped box.

Harrison wanted to open the box right away. But Dad said, "First we make a birthday team!" Everyone held hands in a big circle. Milo counted, and they all sang the birthday song. Grandma carried in the cake. Three little candles stood on top. Grandma lit them with a match, far from Harrison's hands.

"Make a wish," said Mom. Harrison puffed his cheeks and blew. The little flames went out! He blew air, and the candles went dark. He clapped his hands. "I did that!"

Then came the surprise. Zoe handed him the wrapped box. He tore off the paper. Inside was a tiny puppy puppet with floppy ears. "Woof!" said Harrison. The puppy gave everyone a kiss, and the party team cheered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Emmett sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects.
story:
Emmett ran into the backyard with his new red truck. The sun was warm on his hair. Grandma sat on the step and watched him play.

"Is the grill hot?" Emmett asked.

"Touch nothing," said Grandma. "The grill is hot. Hot things can hurt you."

Emmett looked at the grill. He did not touch it. He put one hand near it instead. The air felt warm. He pulled his hand back fast.

"It is hot because it is on," Emmett said. "Fire makes hot."

Then it began to rain. Little drops fell on the truck. Emmett counted them. One drop, two drops, three drops. He stayed close to Grandma, just like always. They ran under the porch.

The rain made a triangle on the step. It dripped down, one, two, three.

"Rain is cold," said Emmett. "The grill is hot. I only touch the cold rain."

Grandma smiled. "Good thinking, Emmett."

Emmett held out his cupped hands and caught three drops.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Claire is learning to play a musical instrument.
story:
Claire sat by the piano at Miss Rose's studio. She wanted to play a whole song. But her song kept stopping. Her fingers landed on the wrong keys.

"Miss Rose, why does my song stop?" Claire asked.

"Watch my hand," said Miss Rose. She pressed one key down slow. The sound went on and on. Then she lifted her finger. The sound stopped.

Claire looked at the wood keys. She saw it. She pressed a key and held it. The note sang long. She let go too fast. The note stopped fast.

So she tried again. Press and hold. Press and hold. Her fingers stayed on the keys longer now. Her song went from one note to the next. It did not stop in the middle.

At the end, Claire played the whole song all the way. Miss Rose clapped. "Play it one more time," she said.

Claire put her fingers on the keys. "Ready," she said. "One, two, three."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Emma is hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week.
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Emma took her to the park. "One grandma, one week, one park," said Emma. They walked on the bumpy path. Grandma held Emma's hand.

Then Grandma sat down on a bench. "My feet are tired," she said. "Old feet need soft shoes." Emma looked at Grandma's shoes. They were thin and old. Emma knew what to do.

Emma took her coins to the park shop. She would buy soft shoes. The shop man had red slippers. Emma touched them. They felt like a pillow. She bought them for Grandma.

Grandma put them on. She stood up. She walked on the bumpy path. "No more tired feet," said Grandma. Emma heard a happy sound. It was Grandma laughing.

"One grandma, one week, one park," said Emma again. Grandma danced all the way to the swings.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Zoe sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.
story:
Zoe was playing in her room. She smelled something sweet. "Cookies!" said Zoe. But where were they?

She used her eyes to look. One, the hall. Two, the kitchen. No cookies yet. She used her ears to listen. She heard a small "beep" from the kitchen. That was the oven! She took one step, then another step, down the hall.

Then she used her nose again. The sweet smell got bigger and bigger. The nose knows the way, thought Zoe. She found Dad by the oven. "Can I have one?" she asked. "First they must cool," said Dad.

So Zoe waited. She touched the pan with one finger. It was hot! She pulled her hand back fast. "Hot pan, hot pan," she said. She waited some more.

At last Dad gave her a warm cookie in a cup. She took a little bite. Her tongue said yum! "I am so lucky," said Zoe. "My nose found the cookies, and my tongue gets to eat them."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Caleb is learning something new. What Caleb is learning: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more.
story:
Caleb sat at the little red table. Miss Jo put down two bowls of blocks. "Which bowl has more?" she asked. Caleb wanted to win the big star sticker. He had to get it right.

He counted the first bowl. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted the other bowl. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six was more. He pointed. "This one!"

But Caleb wanted to check. He counted the six bowl again, starting from the other side. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six again! He giggled. "Same number!" He pushed the bowl. It wobbled, but every block stayed put. "Cool," said Caleb. "They stick like glue."

Miss Jo laughed. "Here is your star." Caleb stuck it on his shirt. He counted the points. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted them backwards. "Five, four, three, two, one. Still five!"

Miss Jo clapped. Caleb grinned and said, "Counting is my best idea."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Aiden is learning something new. What Aiden is learning: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done.
story:
Aiden sat in his cozy chair. He wanted to draw a cat for Grandma. But the tablet was dark. The screen showed nothing at all. Aiden tapped it. Still dark. He tapped again. Still dark. "Oh no," said Aiden. Then Mom showed him one small button on the side. Aiden pressed it. The screen lit up bright. Aiden's eyes went wide. One little press, and the light came on. Aiden pressed the button one more time. The screen went dark again. He pressed it once more. Bright again. "It listens to my finger," said Aiden.

He set the tablet on his knee. He tapped the green square, one tap. The drawing app opened. Aiden drew a cat. He drew one ear, two ears, one tail. He drew four small paws. "A cat for Grandma," he said. Just then his eyes felt sleepy. The sun began to sink outside the window. Mom put a blanket on his shoulders.

"All done," said Aiden. He did not leave the tablet on the chair. He pressed the small button. The screen went dark. He carried the tablet with two hands. He set it in the basket, right next to the books. "Night night, tablet," said Aiden. Mom kissed his head. The tablet rested in the basket, dark and still.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Emma is hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week.
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Emma wanted to show her the park. "We can buy bread for the ducks," said Emma. So they did.

At the park, they sat on a bumpy bench. Emma dropped one crumb. Plop. One duck swam over fast. She dropped more crumbs. Plop, plop, plop. Now two ducks came, then three. "Look, Grandma!" said Emma. "The crumbs bring the ducks!" The ducks made a funny sound. Quack, quack, quack.

Every day that week, Emma and Grandma walked to the park. One crumb, one duck. More crumbs, more ducks. "Again!" said Emma. Grandma laughed and tore the bread. The ducks came closer and closer. Emma counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five ducks!" Grandma clapped her hands. "More bread," said Emma, "for duck number six!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Axel is planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow.
story:
Axel had a small red pot. He wanted to grow a carrot. Papa helped him put dirt in the pot. Axel dropped in one tiny seed. Then he patted the dirt, soft and brown.

Every morning, Axel ran to the balcony. "Hello, pot!" he said. But nothing grew. Axel felt mad. His bottom lip went down, down, down. "Where is my carrot?" he asked. Papa touched the dry dirt. "The dirt is very dry," he said. "The seed is thirsty."

So Axel got his little blue cup. He poured water on the dirt. Drip, drip, drip. He did it every day. Water the seed, water the seed.

One morning, Axel saw something green. A small leaf was poking up! Axel clapped his hands. He ran to tell his teacher, who lived next door. "My seed woke up!" he called. "It does not sleep anymore!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Aubrey is learning something new. What Aubrey is learning: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each.
story:
Aubrey was at the farm with Grandpa. She wanted to help him feed the animals. Grandpa said, "First, let's play a little game."

Grandpa held up a red apple. "What do you use to see this?" Aubrey looked and looked. Then she covered her eyes with her hands. The apple was gone! She moved her hands. The apple came back. "My eyes!" she said.

Next, Grandpa rang the big cowbell. Aubrey covered her ears. The sound got small. She moved her hands away. The sound got big again. "My ears!" she said.

Then Grandpa let her touch a soft yellow chick. "My hands feel it," she said. She smelled fresh bread in the farm kitchen. "My nose smells it!" Then she took a tiny bite of apple. "My tongue tastes it!"

Grandpa smiled. "Now we can feed the animals." Aubrey patted the tired old horse. The horse looked at her with big gentle eyes.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Everly sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations.
story:
Everly ran to the sandbox. Her friend Mia was there. Mia had a little toy bear and a pink cup. "I am playing house," said Mia. "My bear is sick."

Everly wanted to play too. But she had no cup. She looked down. She felt worried she could not join.

Then Everly saw a stick. She picked it up. She held it like a spoon. "This can be my spoon," she said. She stirred the sand. The stick worked because it was pretend. You can pretend a stick is anything.

She fed the bear tiny sand cakes. "Open your mouth, little bear," she said. The bear got a quick drink from the pink cup.

"Dad, can a stick be a spoon?" Everly asked. Dad smiled from the bench. "In pretend play, yes."

Everly stirred and stirred. The bear felt all better.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Aubrey is learning something new. What Aubrey is learning: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each.
story:
Aubrey went to the farm with Grandpa. She wanted to name five senses. Grandpa said, "Take your time. We can find them all."

First she found the sheep. She touched the soft wool. "Touching is a sense!" she said. "My skin does that." Next she heard the rooster. "Hearing is a sense. My ears do that." Then she smelled fresh bread. "My nose does smelling!" She ate a warm piece. "My tongue tastes it."

Aubrey was getting tired. She looked and looked. "I need one more." Then she saw the big red barn. She laughed. "I used my eyes! I see with my eyes. My eyes found it!"

Grandpa clapped his hands. "Five senses, all found."

Aubrey yawned and said, "My tired feet need the car."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Asher sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them.
story:
Asher ran into the backyard. The sun felt warm on his face. "It is sunny today," he said. He wore his yellow t-shirt and shorts. His hat sat on the bench. Asher put on his hat. The sun was too bright without it.

Then the wind began to blow. It blew Asher's hat right off. The hat rolled across the grass. Asher chased it. The wind pushed it under the bush. The hat was stuck. Asher pulled and pulled. Out it came, at last. "That was a big wind," he said.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. Asher ran inside. Mom helped him put on his raincoat and boots. He took his blue bucket outside. The rain fell into the bucket. Soon it was full. Asher put his hand in the water. "I can make my toy boat swim," he said. He floated the little boat in the bucket.

The rain stopped. The sky got cold and white. Soft snow began to fall. Asher put on his warm coat and mittens. He caught one snowflake on his mitten. It sat there, small and white. He looked up at the sky. "More, please," he whispered. The snow kept falling, soft and slow.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Mackenzie is learning to ride a bike without training wheels.
story:
Mackenzie stood in the empty schoolyard. Her bike had no training wheels now. Dad held the seat behind her.

"You can push the pedals fast," said Dad. Mackenzie pushed the pedals. The bike wobbled. She fell into the soft grass.

She tried again. Slow pedals made the bike tip side to side. "Hmm," said Mackenzie. "What happens if I go fast?" She pushed hard on the pedals. The wheels spun quick and round. The bike went straight. It stopped wobbling!

"Faster makes it steady!" she called. Dad let go of the seat. He ran behind her toward the house across the field. Mackenzie did not look back. She looked at her fast spinning wheels.

"I did my first big ride!" she shouted. Dad clapped and clapped.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Olivia is learning to swim at the local pool.
story:
Olivia brought her towel to the pool. Grandpa brought her goggles. "Time to swim," he said.

Olivia held the wall and kicked her legs. Kick, kick, kick. The water splashed up. Some water went in her mouth. It tasted funny. "Sorry, water," she said, and she spit it out. "Why did that happen?" she wondered.

Grandpa blew a big breath out into the water. Bubbles came up. Pop, pop, pop. Olivia tried it. She put her mouth near the water. She blew out, and bubbles popped on top. No water came in her mouth! She blew again. Bubbles, and no water. "The bubbles push the water away," she said. "Blowing out keeps the water out."

Then she kicked and blew bubbles at the same time. She let go of the wall. Her arms paddled. She was swimming! A bubble popped right on her nose. It tickled. Olivia laughed, and Grandpa laughed too.

"Look at me, Grandpa!" she called. "Bubble, bubble, splash!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Jake is attending a religious or cultural celebration with family.
story:
Grandma's house smelled like potato pancakes. It was Hanukkah! Jake jumped up and down. Grandpa put the menorah on the table.

"Can I light one?" Jake asked. "Not alone," said Grandpa. "The flame is hot." Jake made a sad face. Then Grandpa held out his big hand. "We can do it together."

Grandpa's hand held Jake's little hand. Together they held the helper candle. They touched it to a small candle. A flame popped up! Everyone clapped. Jake watched the candle burn. The wax at the top began to melt, drop by drop. "The fire makes it melt!" Jake said. Grandpa laughed. "Yes, it does."

Grandma gave Jake a warm pancake. Jake took a big bite. "More candles tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes," said Grandpa. "One more every night." Jake grinned and clapped for the flame.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Willow sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help.
story:
Willow wanted her red crayon. It was on the top shelf. The shelf was too tall. She stood on her toes. She stretched her arm up high. The crayon did not move.

Willow climbed onto a little stool. She reached again. The crayon wobbled and fell. It hit her brother's block tower. The tower fell down too. Crash! The blocks rolled across the tidy floor.

Willow felt bad about the tower. She looked at her brother. "Sorry," she said. "I broke your tower." Her brother nodded. "Let's fix it together," he said. Willow smiled. She handed him the big blocks. He stacked them one by one.

Then Willow pointed up high. "Can you help me, please?" she asked. Her brother reached the red crayon. He put it in her hand. "Thank you!" said Willow. She drew a big red sun. Her brother drew a red house. They sat side by side on the floor. "Nice sun," said her brother.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Oliver is reading a whole book alone for the first time.
story:
Oliver sat in Grandma's sunny room. He had a little book about a pink pig. He wanted to read it all by himself.

"I can do it," he said. "One letter, then another."

He pointed at the first word. P. I. G. He said each letter out loud. Then he pushed the sounds together. "Pig!" The word popped out like magic. The picture on the page was a pink pig. It matched!

He turned the page. C. O. W. He pushed the sounds together. "Cow!" There was the cow. Page after page, he went. Pig, cow, hen, duck. He named them all. "One animal, then another," he said.

On the last page, there was a surprise. A tiny pink mouse was hiding in the hay. Oliver laughed. The mouse was not in his naming. But he could read its name. M. O. U. S. E. "Mouse!"

He ran to the kitchen. "Grandma! I read a whole book!" he did not need to yell, but he did anyway, because he was so happy. Grandma clapped her hands.

Grandma picked him up and spun him around. "A whole book," she said. "All by yourself." Oliver hugged the little book to his chest. Outside, the sun went down, pink and soft. Oliver said, "Tomorrow, can I read two books?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Lydia sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations.
story:
Lydia got to daycare early. The play kitchen stood empty in the corner. She wanted to play house with her friend Mia. But Mia was not there yet.

Lydia found the baby doll on the floor. The doll had no blanket. Lydia thought the baby must be cold. She wrapped the doll in a soft red cloth. She patted the baby's back, pat, pat.

Then Mia came in. "Can I be the big sister?" asked Mia. "Yes," said Lydia. "You can feed the baby." Mia held a tiny cup to the doll's mouth. "Drink your milk," said Mia. The doll's shirt got a little wet. "The milk spills out," said Lydia. "The baby can't really drink. It is just pretend."

The baby still needed a nap. Lydia and Mia rocked the doll. They hummed a quiet song. The room smelled like crayons and warm toast.

The baby's eyes stayed open. "Babies need us to close their eyes," said Lydia. She gently laid the doll down. "Shh," whispered Mia. "Night night, baby."

activity: Mackenzie is learning to ride a bike without training wheels.
story:
Mackenzie stood by her house with her bike. Dad had taken off the training wheels. "This is my first try," she said.

She sat on the seat. Dad gave a little push. Mackenzie pedaled slow. The bike went wobble, wobble. Then it fell over. "Why did it tip?" she wondered.

She looked at her big brother. He rode fast. His bike did not tip at all. Hmm. Maybe fast feet help?

Mackenzie got back on. Dad gave a big push. This time she pedaled fast, fast, fast. Her feet went round and round like wheels. The bike did not wobble! It went straight down the path.

"Fast feet make the bike stand up!" she called. She rode past the swings. She rode past the big tree. She did not fall once.

At the end of the path she turned around and rode back. "Watch me, Dad! Watch my fast feet!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Charlotte is learning something new. What Charlotte is learning: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes.
story:
Charlotte sat in the school library. She wanted to find a book about horses. But she could not read the letters yet.

Mrs. Bell handed her a card. The card had one big letter on it. The letter was H.

"H says huh, like horse," said Mrs. Bell.

Charlotte tapped the card. "Huh," she said. Then she opened a book and pointed. "Huh, huh, huh!"

The first word she tapped was horse. The picture showed a big brown horse.

"I found it!" said Charlotte.

Next to her, a boy named Sam spilled his crayons on the floor. Charlotte picked them up. One crayon rolled under the shelf.

"Here," she said, handing it back. Then she saw his boot. The word on the page in her head was B. "B says buh," she told him. "Buh, buh, boot!"

Sam laughed. Charlotte turned the page.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Myles sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting.
story:
Myles sat at the dinner table. He wanted the bread, but it was far away. "Please pass the bread," said Myles. Daddy pushed the plate to him.

Daddy began to count the peas. "One, two, three, four, five." Myles listened. The words went in a line, like a little song. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten," said Daddy. Then he ate a pea.

Myles picked up his spoon. He wanted to count too. "One, two, three," said Myles. He touched a pea with each word. "Four, five, six." But then he stopped. He did not know what came next. He squeezed his lips and thought hard.

His big sister Tessa smiled at him. She was friendly that way. She wiped her hands on the towel. Then she leaned over and whispered, "Seven." Myles beamed. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" He touched the last four peas, one word for each.

"Ten peas," said Myles. "Ten words, ten peas!" He put all ten in his mouth at once. His cheeks went big and round like two little moons. Daddy laughed. Tessa laughed too. Then Myles counted his carrots. He did not need help this time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Milo is going on a family trip away from home.
story:
Milo sat on the big train. He was going on a trip with Mama and Papa. He wanted to look out the window and see a pig.

The train went into a tunnel. It got dark. Then Milo's ears went pop. They felt funny and stuffy. "My ears hurt," he said.

Mama said, "Try a sip of your juice." Milo took a big sip. He made a funny face. The juice was sour. But then his ears went pop again, and they felt better.

"Why did that help?" Milo asked. Mama said, "The sipping made your ears open."

The train came out of the tunnel. It was bright again. Milo looked out the window. He saw a pink pig by a fence. "The tunnel made my ears pop," said Milo. "The sip fixed them." Mama smiled and clapped.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Theo is learning something new. What Theo is learning: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes.
story:
Theo sat on the small red rug at school. Miss Ana held up a card. It had a letter on it. The letter was T.

"What sound does T make?" asked Miss Ana.

Theo looked down at the bottom of his shoe. He did not know. His friend Mia said, "Tuh, tuh, T!"

At play time, Theo found the letter basket. He pulled out a big wooden T. He turned it over in his hands. Then he set it on the table. It stood up tall.

"Tuh," he said, just to try it.

Then something funny happened. His mouth popped a little puff of air. He felt it on his hand. He said it again. "Tuh." Another puff, cool and soft, on his fingers. The letter made his mouth do that.

Miss Ana came over. "Say it once more," she said.

Theo held up the wooden T. "Tuh." The puff touched his hand again. He laughed.

Theo tapped the T on the table. "Tuh, tuh, tuh," he said. "Theo starts with T. My name makes the puff too."

"Yes it does," said Miss Ana. "T is for Theo."

At home time, Theo ran to his dad with his closed fists. He opened one hand. A paper T sat inside it.

"Listen," Theo said. He held it near his mouth. "Tuh." He smiled at the little puff in the air.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Luke sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the idea that plants and animals need food, water and a place to live.
story:
Luke had a big sunflower in a pot. It stood by the window. But today its leaves hung down. They looked sad and soft.

Luke touched the dirt. It was dry and crumbly. He ran to get his small watering can. He filled it at the sink. Mom held the faucet so the water would not splash. Luke poured the water slowly. The dirt drank it up with a soft sip, sip, sip.

Then Luke saw something. A little brown bird sat on the sill. It hop, hopped along the ledge. It pecked at nothing. There was no seed there.

"Are you hungry?" Luke asked. He got the seed box. He sprinkled seeds on the tray outside the window. The bird flew down. It pecked and pecked. Luke heard the tiny tap, tap of its beak.

That night the sunflower stood tall again. Its leaves lifted up toward the light. The bird had found a spot to sleep in the big tree. Luke climbed into his own bed. He pulled the blanket up to his chin.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Milo is going on a family trip away from home.
story:
Milo sat on the train with his mama. He was going on a big trip to Grandma's house. But Milo could not see out the window. The curtain was closed. "I want to see the pigs," said Milo. Mama tried to slide the curtain, but it stuck. Milo pulled the fabric with both hands. It did not move. He pulled again, slow and gentle. The curtain slid across with a soft whoosh. The window was open to the sun!

"Look, Mama, I did it," said Milo. Now he could see the fields. Cows stood by a fence. Then Milo saw a pink pig in the mud. "Pig! Pig!" he shouted. The pig rolled over and stood up. Milo laughed.

Mama gave him a lemon drop from her bag. Milo sucked on it. "It tastes sour," he said, and he made a funny face. Mama laughed too. Milo held the curtain open with one hand. He did not want the window to hide again. The train went clickety-clack. Milo watched for more pigs all the way.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Emmett sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects.
story:
Emmett ran into the backyard. Dad was by the grill. The grill was hot. Emmett could feel it from far away. "Can I touch the grill?" Emmett asked. "No," said Dad. "It is hot. Hot things can hurt you." So Emmett stood back with Dad.

Emmett saw Dad put a sandwich on the grill. It was a triangle. One side got brown lines. Then the other side got brown lines. Dad flipped it with a long tool. Emmett counted the flips. One flip. Two flips. Three flips. "Dad, why do you use the long tool?" asked Emmett. "So my hand stays far from the hot part," said Dad.

Then the sky got dark. Drops began to rain down. Emmett and Dad ran to the porch. They ate the warm triangle sandwich together. It was crunchy and good. "Tomorrow we can cook again," said Dad. Emmett smiled and took a big bite of his new favorite lunch.
